results.authors: Biller J, Sacco RL, Albuquerque FC, et al.
results.key_finding: Cervical artery dissection is a leading cause of stroke in adults under 45; vertebral dissection presents with posterior neck pain, occipital headache, dizziness and posterior circulation ischemia, and triggers include physical exertion, neck manipulation and minor trauma.
results.title: Cervical arterial dissections and association with cervical manipulative therapy: a statement for healthcare professionals from the American Heart Association/American Stroke Association

results.authors: CADISS trial investigators (Markus HS, Hayter E, Levi C, et al.)
results.key_finding: In extracranial carotid and vertebral dissection, stroke recurrence at 3 months was low (about 2%) and did not differ between antiplatelet and anticoagulant treatment; intracranial dissection was not studied.
results.title: Antiplatelet treatment compared with anticoagulation treatment for cervical artery dissection (CADISS): a randomised trial

results.authors: Kleindorfer DO, Towfighi A, Chaturvedi S, et al.
results.key_finding: In patients with stroke or TIA and extracranial carotid or vertebral artery dissection, antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy for at least 3 months is reasonable (COR 2a).
results.title: 2021 Guideline for the Prevention of Stroke in Patients With Stroke and Transient Ischemic Attack: A Guideline From the American Heart Association/American Stroke Association

output.summary: Antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy have not been shown to differ in extracranial cervical artery dissection, and guidelines accept either for at least 3 months. The trials and the recommendation do not cover intradural (intracranial) dissection, where anticoagulation is usually avoided because of the risk of subarachnoid haemorrhage. Follow-up vessel imaging at 3 to 6 months assesses recanalization.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not start anticoagulation for this dissection: it extends into the intradural V4 segment, with a risk of subarachnoid hemorrhage.
Do not perform lumbar puncture: CT within 6 hours of the headache shows no subarachnoid blood, and the cerebellar infarct with fourth ventricular effacement carries a risk of herniation.

Do not start or restart antihypertensive treatment in the first 48 to 72 hours for blood pressure below 220/120 mmHg in a patient who receives neither IV thrombolysis nor thrombectomy and has no comorbid indication; it does not prevent death or dependency (AHA/ASA 2026, COR 3: No Benefit).
Do not attribute the thunderclap occipital headache to benign musculoskeletal gym injury without cerebrovascular imaging.
required_recommendations: Establish last known well (onset during the squat, about 2 hours before arrival; the intermittent prodromal symptoms of the previous 3 days do not move it) and the NIHSS (2: limb ataxia 2; gait ataxia is not scored).

IV thrombolysis: do not give. He is within 4.5 hours and the gait ataxia is disabling, but the dissection extends into the intradural V4 segment, where thrombolysis risks subarachnoid hemorrhage and its usefulness is not established (uncertain benefit in the guideline); withholding it is the safer choice for a deficit limited to right limb and gait ataxia (NIHSS 2). Thrombectomy: not indicated (near-occlusion of the distal right vertebral artery with the basilar and left vertebral arteries patent; no basilar occlusion).

Start aspirin (for example 300 mg once, then 75 to 100 mg daily) for at least 3 months and do not anticoagulate: the dissection extends intradurally (V4), where anticoagulation risks subarachnoid hemorrhage. CADISS and the AHA/ASA recommendation of antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy (COR 2a) cover extracranial dissection only.

Admit to a stroke unit with continuous cardiac monitoring (telemetry) for at least the first 24 hours and frequent neurological checks for cerebellar swelling (infarct 2.8 x 2.1 cm, fourth ventricle mildly effaced): repeat imaging on any decline in consciousness and involve neurosurgery early for ventriculostomy or suboccipital decompression if hydrocephalus or brainstem compression develops.
Stop ibuprofen (it blunts the antiplatelet effect of aspirin and adds bleeding risk); use acetaminophen for headache and neck pain.
Repeat non-invasive vessel imaging (CTA or MRA) at 3 to 6 months to assess recanalization or pseudoaneurysm and to decide the duration of antithrombotic therapy.
Advise against heavy weightlifting, straining and neck manipulation until follow-up vessel imaging shows healing.

Start atorvastatin 80 mg daily: LDL 118 mg/dL after a non-cardioembolic ischaemic stroke without known coronary disease meets the AHA/ASA 2021 secondary prevention indication (COR 1, SPARCL), although the mechanism is the vertebral dissection rather than atherosclerosis; target LDL below 70 mg/dL.

key_clinical_evidence: Thunderclap occipital headache during heavy exertion with right-sided neck pain, vertigo, vomiting, right limb ataxia and inability to walk is a posterior circulation syndrome until proven otherwise; CT first excludes cerebellar and subarachnoid hemorrhage.
NIHSS is 2 (limb ataxia 2). Gait and truncal ataxia are not scored on the NIHSS, so a low score understates the disability of a cerebellar stroke in a patient who cannot walk.
Prodromal right neck pain and intermittent dizziness for 3 days before the stroke are a recognized warning pattern of vertebral artery dissection.

The intramural hematoma is T1-hyperintense (subacute) while the infarct is hyperacute: the dissection began with the neck pain about 3 days earlier, so a subacute hematoma with a hyperacute infarct is expected.

CTA and MRI place the dissection from V3 into the intradural V4 segment, which explains the absent PICA opacification and changes management: the evidence for antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy (CADISS, AHA/ASA COR 2a) covers extracranial dissection only, and anticoagulation is avoided intradurally for the risk of subarachnoid hemorrhage.
Extracranial dissection is not a contraindication to IV thrombolysis, but intradural extension makes its benefit uncertain and carries a subarachnoid hemorrhage risk; here it is not given.
No basilar occlusion: the basilar and left vertebral arteries are patent, so thrombectomy is not indicated.
A cerebellar infarct of 2.8 x 2.1 cm with fourth ventricular effacement needs monitoring for swelling and early neurosurgical involvement for ventriculostomy or suboccipital decompression.
CRP 1.4 mg/dL and ESR 22 mm/hr two hours after onset are nonspecific and do not point to vasculitis in the absence of systemic features.

metadata.condition_name: Acute ischemic stroke (right vertebral artery dissection)
metadata.difficulty_description: Moderate — posterior circulation stroke in a young adult with an exertional trigger. Prodromal neck pain dismissed as musculoskeletal strain is a red herring. Mild inflammatory markers and elevated LDL add confounders. The diagnosis requires recognizing posterior fossa cerebellar signs, ordering vascular imaging for dissection, and distinguishing this from SAH (thunderclap headache), vestibular neuritis, and atherosclerotic vertebrobasilar disease.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Required: NCCT, admission bloods, ECG, CTA and the ibuprofen drug check; MRI with DWI and fat-saturated T1, echocardiogram and rhythm monitoring recommended. Three red herrings (inflammatory markers, LDL, musculoskeletal anchor); the agent must recognize the intradural extension and its consequences for thrombolysis and anticoagulation, and actively exclude SAH and vestibular mimics.
metadata.real_seed_note: Seeded from: Shi Q et al. Cerebellar infarction caused by vertebral artery dissection: A case report. Medicine (Baltimore). 2023;102(24):e33987. PMID 37327265. PMC10270511. CC-BY 4.0. Confirmed right vertebral artery dissection (V1/V3-V4 segments) with right cerebellar ischemic infarction in a 34-year-old male triggered by barbell squat exercise. Core mechanism, vessel, laterality, and exertional trigger preserved; demographics, presentation, full clinical workup, imaging, tool outputs, and ground truth are original authorship for NeuroBench v5.
metadata.revision_reason: Independent Reviewer 2 stroke audit: NCCT and CTA separated; MRI optional; CTP routed only to two extended-window cases; routine MRA/TCD/duplex duplication removed; acute labs carry explicit do-not-delay rules; EEG retained for one seizure-mimic case

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Wei Chen is a 34-year-old right-handed East Asian man with no significant medical history who presents to the emergency department via ambulance approximately 2 hours after the acute onset of severe occipital headache, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, right limb incoordination, and inability to walk steadily. The symptoms began abruptly during heavy barbell squat exercise at the gym, with a sharp 'thunderclap-like' posterior headache as the initiating event. He reports that over the preceding 3 days he had experienced intermittent dizziness, right-sided neck pain, and transient blurred vision, which he attributed to overexertion and a muscle strain from the gym. He dismissed these prodromal symptoms and continued exercising. Today, while completing a squat with approximately 100 kg on the barbell, he felt a sudden explosive pain at the back of his head radiating into the right side of his neck, immediately followed by severe dizziness, nausea, vomiting, and the sensation that the room was spinning. His gym partner noted that he appeared unsteady and was staggering to the right. Mr. Chen was unable to walk a straight line and was brought to the floor carefully by his training partner. An ambulance was called. He denies any loss of consciousness, facial weakness, arm or leg weakness, difficulty speaking or understanding speech, or visual field loss. He has no prior history of migraines or similar headaches. He denies any prior neck trauma, chiropractic manipulation, or recent upper respiratory tract infection. He is otherwise healthy, takes no regular prescription medications, and uses ibuprofen occasionally for gym-related neck stiffness. He denies any illicit drug use. He has never had symptoms like this before.

neurological_exam.additional: NIHSS score: 2 (limb ataxia 2: right arm and right leg; all other items 0; gait ataxia is not scored). Severe occipital headache and right posterior neck pain rated 7/10. No meningismus. No carotid bruits. No Marfan habitus or joint hypermobility. Patient reports onset of symptoms approximately 2 hours ago during vigorous barbell squat exercise at the gym. He had a prodromal episode of intermittent dizziness and right-sided neck pain over the preceding 3 days, which he attributed to a gym-related muscle strain.
